title: Short Stuff: Christmas Cards
summary: Short Stuff Christmas Week episode on the history of Christmas cards, suggested by listener Robert Paulson. Covers Sir Henry Cole, who commissioned John Callcott Horsley to design the first Christmas card in 1843 to cope with the volume of holiday letters he received; Victorian letter-writing customs; how Christmas cards caught on by the 1860s alongside the Penny Post, Dickens's A Christmas Carol, and Christmas's rising popularity; Louis Prang's first American Christmas cards in 1873; the gimcrack era that replaced cards for about two decades; later revival through cameras, offset printing, and Hallmark's artist-commissioned cards; Hallmark's Three Little Angels; and the environmental cost of Christmas cards with eco-friendly alternatives and opting out.
topics: A Christmas Carol influence on Christmas

segments.title: Intro and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Christmas Week Short Stuff and thank listener Robert Paulson, who suggested the topic of Christmas cards as a holiday gift.

segments.title: Sir Henry Cole and the first Christmas card
segments.summary: Sir Henry Cole, a civil servant and early industrial design figure who founded the V&A in 1852, was overwhelmed by holiday letters. He had Horsley design a card, and in 1843 sent the first Christmas cards.

segments.title: Victorian reaction and adoption
segments.summary: The Victorians initially objected to cards lacking the news of letters, but the cards caught on by the 1860s.

segments.title: Penny Post, Dickens, and spread to America
segments.summary: Cole helped pass the Penny Post, and A Christmas Carol helped shape Christmas. Louis Prang introduced American Christmas cards in 1873 in Roxbury, Massachusetts.

segments.title: Gimcracks, revival, and famous artists
segments.summary: Gimcracks replaced cards for about twenty years, then cards returned with cameras and better printing. Hallmark and others commissioned artists including Dali, Rockwell, Grandma Moses, and Jackie Kennedy.

segments.title: Three Little Angels and digital alternatives
segments.summary: Hallmark's Three Little Angels is the best-selling Christmas card, with about thirty-four million copies sold. Digital cards are now an alternative.

segments.title: Environmental impact and greener options
segments.summary: About 2.5 billion holiday cards are sold in the US yearly. Suggestions include postcards, recycled or wood-based paper, avoiding glossy or metallic finishes, and asking contacts to stop sending cards.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts mention a family's Christmas newsletter and wish listeners a merry Christmas and happy holidays.
